1273.note: The cipher letter is Olivares to the Duke of Alba, Madrid 22 Aug 1626 (BNE MSS/10249 ff. 13-15, five sides of cipher, no gloss on the leaves), but DECODE R1190 is this very letter with status 'Decrypted' (Cryptoole ES1626-1 'solved'), so it has been read by others although I could not see the plaintext.

seen.where: BNE Digital viewer for MSS/10249 'Papeles varios' (card https://bnedigital.bne.es/bd/card?oid=0000042230&site=bdh, 64 images, shelfmark MSS/10249, 57 h.), openings 14-19 viewed whole and zoomed in Chrome on 4 Nov 2026; no check page appeared on bnedigital.bne.es.
seen.extent: ff. 13r-15r: five sides of continuous cipher, about 22 lines on f.13r and about 25-30 lines on each of f.13v, f.14r, f.14v and f.15r, ending with the clear dateline 'de Madrid a 22 de Agosto 1626' (last digit read as 6) and the autograph signature 'Don Gaspar de Guzman'; docket 'Duque de Alba'. f.12r is a separate clear covering letter of the same date to the Duke of Alba ('En los negocios publicos vera VE lo que se ofrece por los despachos ...'), not a decipherment.
seen.cipher: Whole body of the letter in a mixed cipher: dotted numbers (e.g. 10, 16, 36, 97), short letter groups (fer, xer, pon, hi, tor ...) and a few signs, written continuously with full stops between groups. No plaintext, interlinear gloss, marginal note or key is written on or beside ff. 13-15; only faint show-through from the reverse. The BNE card notes 'Una de las cartas del Conde Duque al Duque de Alba (h. 13-15) es cifrada'. The lead's 'undated' is wrong: the letter is dated 22 Aug 1626.

No plaintext or key file is shown on the record page. The lead's 'Not on DECODE' is therefore wrong. The harvested dumps in the repo do not contain R1190; research/cryptoole/snapshot.json lists it as decode:1190 / ES1626-1 with status 'solved'.

1405.note: The Fanning Island telegram of 11 Jan 1918 is a run of two-letter groups (VE UT UW RX DE ... AR MY OW VE) that the Navy Radio Service itself read as ship call-sign and procedure signals (a ship 'intermingling Naval Service procedure with Commercial Signalling procedure'), later put down to Japanese ships' high-speed transmitters, with DE and AR being the Morse procedure signs; no cipher or decipherment is on the file.

seen.where: NAA RecordSearch MP1049/1, 1914/0467, item 405327 (Wireless telegraphy intercepted messages 1914-1918 War, 705 pages), images served at https://recordsearch.naa.gov.au/SearchNRetrieve/NAAMedia/ShowImage.aspx?B=405327&T=P&S=5 to S=10 (S=5/8 the telegram, S=7 memorandum, S=9 minute paper, S=10 letter), viewed in Chrome 4 Nov 2026 without any check page; only these pages of the 705 were looked at.
seen.extent: One 'Copy of Telegram', Officer-in-Charge Fanning Island Radio to Navy Office, sent 0220 and received 2400, 11 Jan 1918: 'Following groups received 11.55 p.m. 900 metres quenched high frequency spark signals strength three', then a single typed line of about 12-14 two-letter groups beginning VE UT UW RX DE and ending ... AR MY OW VE, one group with a slashed first character, note 'Letter E in 19th text is accented'.
seen.cipher: Not a cipher on the file's own evidence. The Radio Service memorandum of 14 Jan 1918 (S=7) says the signals are 'of a suspicious nature', that the ship 'is apparently trying to intermingle Naval Service procedure with Commercial Signalling procedure' on a Telefunken quenched spark set 'such as would be used by a Raider', or that they 'may turn out to be signals made by American Stations', and asks for American naval call signs. The minute paper of 10 Apr 1918 (S=9) records that the US Consul General says they do not come from American stations and concludes they come from Japanese ships with high-speed transmitters or the new Java station; no action. A Post and Telegraph Dept letter of 6 Mar 1918 (S=10) concerns 'automatic arc signals heard by Wellington Radio'. DE and AR are standard Morse procedure signals ('from', 'end of message'). No decipherment or plaintext is written on or with the telegram, and no key or code is cited.
